## 2026-10-11 ARV-119 Weekly summary figures per site and local week (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1; passes true)
- Plan: the weekly figures only (the owner's decision of 2026-10-08 moved templates, documents, CSV, schedules, delivery and any endpoint to ARV-146): a pure builder in Ariva.Core/Reports fed by one reader of stored rows, served by a site-scoped service returning `Result<WeeklySummary>`, shaped as plain records (no value tuples) so ARV-146 can hand it on as JSON. CWEs: CWE-863 (site scope, per-role projection, border per-desk data), CWE-120 (one week per request, every read bounded and refused beyond its bound), with CWE-89 (constant, parameterised SQL).
- Built: `WeeklySummary` and its records, `WeeklySummaryInput`, `WeeklySummaryLimits` and `WeeklySummaries` (calendar, week check, build) in Ariva.Core/Reports; `ISvcWeeklySummary` and `WeeklySummaryErrors` in Ariva.Core/Services/Reports; `WeeklySummaryReader` and `SvcWeeklySummary` in Ariva.Infra/Services/Reports; `AvailabilityLedgerReader` (the ledger's per-day query moved out of `SvcAvailability` unchanged, so the availability read and the summary count alike); `DailyReports.Uptime` made internal for the week; registrations in `AccountExtensions` (Ariva.Api.Main). No endpoint, no script, nothing stored. The local week is computed in .NET (`SiteTimeZones`, the daily report's `DayBounds`) and handed to PostgreSQL as hour and day bounds, grouped with `width_bucket`, so a Berlin autumn week has 169 hours and PostgreSQL's time zone data never decides a day; minute histograms are merged per lane, hour and bucket in the database (at most one row per lane and hour), percentiles taken in .NET by F7.
- Proposed points for the owner: docs/product/decisions.md, ARV-119 entry, points (1) to (13), and an Open decisions row (Monday weeks in the site's zone, a site with an unknown zone refused; peak hours by the daily report's rule and the site's ten worst lane-hours; time to acknowledge over acknowledged alerts only; device uptime as the daily report; data quality from the latest bin revisions with track completion from the sums; overflow minutes read from `overflow_minute` with the view's rule; desk-state lane totals for every reader with small border lanes withheld; the service's own `Report.View` check; the bounds).

## 2026-10-11 ARV-122 split into ARV-122a and ARV-122b (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Why: the engineer's survey before any code found the story too big for one session (two endpoints, the bundle builder and checker, seven importers reusing the existing checks, the floor plan sanitiser again, the site lock, a new permission, about 11 E2E cases, concurrency tests) and three points no rule settled. ARV-122a carries the bundle format, export, the manifest check, the permission, and the import of the topology, desk code mappings, the draft profile and floor plans; ARV-122b adds devices, alert rules and displays. ARV-137 now depends on ARV-122b.
- Owner decisions (2026-10-11): (1) the geometry hash F22 v1 names levels and desks by their database ids, so no import can reproduce it; v1 stays unchanged (campaigns, frozen results, devices and evidence packs quote it) and a portable geometry hash, computed on request and never stored, names them by their codes; the round trip compares the portable hash. (2) Imported alert rules and displays are checked against the imported draft profile's zones with the same rules; they act only once it is published. (3) An alert rule's escalation contact (free text that may name a person) is never exported; the import answer lists the rules that need one.
- Lead's calls (Proposed, for decisions.md): a display code already taken in the target database answers 409; the bundle names its airport by IATA code, which must already exist on the target and is never created; device calibrations are never exported.

## 2026-10-12 ARV-158 Display texts judged per code point (DisplayText.IsClean) (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- What changed: `DisplayText.IsClean` (Ariva.Core/Domain/Components/DisplayText.cs) walks the text once with `Rune.DecodeFromUtf16`: a lone surrogate is refused first (a high surrogate at the end included), then any control or format character per code point (`Rune.IsControl`, category Format), so the tag characters (U+E0001, U+E0020 to U+E007F), the shorthand format controls (U+1BCA0 to U+1BCA3) and musical formatting (U+1D173 to U+1D17A) are refused behind every `Require` and `Optional` like a right-to-left override; `allowLineBreaks` unchanged; in the basic plane a rune and a char are judged alike, so every basic plane text keeps its result. No schema change; the CHECK classes of scripts 0020 and 0022 stay basic plane only (immutable; parity left to a new script, ARV-157 or later).
- Tests: unit `DisplayTextTests` (U+E0041 inside a text, U+E0001, U+1D173 and U+1BCA0 refused; an emoji, Arabic and plain text accepted; the basic plane cases as before; lone surrogates built in a Fact; line breaks with and without `allowLineBreaks`; U+E0041 refused through the alert rule, display, device (model and queue zone name), user display name (`SvcUsers.IsUsableDisplayName`), integration client (constructor and `Rename`) and report schedule entry points). Against the previous `IsClean` the 11 cases with a character outside the basic plane fail and the 10 others pass. Integration `DeviceImportTests.Preview_Should_RefuseTheRowThroughTheRegistration_When_AModelCellHoldsATagCharacter` (site XCII: the reader passes the cell, the registration refuses the row: row 2, no column, `RegistrationRefused`, no token, nothing kept). Every invisible character is an escape; the changed files hold no raw Cf, Mn or Cs character.
- Per-character checks outside `DisplayText` (grep for `char.GetUnicodeCategory`, `CharUnicodeInfo.GetUnicodeCategory`, `char.IsControl`, `char.IsSurrogate`), none changed: Ariva.Infra/Border/AmanPull.cs:185 and Ariva.Infra/Services/Flights/SvcAcrisPull.cs:68 and 69 (control characters stripped from `outbound_endpoint.last_status` and `last_modified`, texts Ariva builds; every control character is in the basic plane, so a check per UTF-16 unit is complete); Ariva.Infra/Notifications/Email.cs:168 and 169 (`Email.Clean` drops every surrogate, so nothing outside the basic plane passes); Ariva.Infra/Imports/CsvImportReader.cs:224 and 236 (control characters only; format characters left to the services, now proved by the integration test); Ariva.Core/Domain/Criteria/ZoneHealthCriteria.cs:37 (a query filter, nothing stored); Platform/Simulation/Ariva.Simulation.Api/Emulators/Validation/ValidationEmulatorSettings.cs:61 and 63 (the emulator's observer settings); already per code point: Ariva.Infra/Services/Topology/SvcFloorPlans.cs:196 (ARV-153) and Ariva.Core/Security/UserNames.cs:25 to 29.
- Gotchas: the subdivision flag emoji (England, Scotland, Wales) are tag sequences and are now refused in every display text (decisions point 2). ## 2026-10-12 ARV-161 Geometry.SegmentsIntersect independent of point order (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- What changed: `Geometry.SegmentsIntersect` (Ariva.Core/Domain/Components/Geometry.cs) puts each segment's ends in a fixed order (by x, then y; negative zero made zero) and then the two segments before any arithmetic, so all eight orders and directions of its arguments compute with the same numbers and give one answer, rounding included. A touch is an end closer than `Tolerance` (1 cm) to the other segment (`DistanceToSegment`, metres against metres); otherwise only a proper crossing counts, with each side 0 when the cross product is below Tolerance times the segment's length (the point's distance to the line, never a cross product against a length). `OnSegment` and the exact-zero test are gone; the 1e-12 `Cross` stays for the neighbour fold-back check of `IsSimplePolygon`, already order-independent. The touch answer is true in every order: a zone vertex on, or within 1 cm of, an edge that is not its own is refused; a footprint touching its zone, or within 1 cm, reaches it (decisions, 2026-10-12 entry, Proposed).
- Tests: unit `GeometryTests` (each segment case in all eight orders: the seed's points, a shared end at the origin 3.5e-14 m apart; 9 mm and 11 mm from the other segment and collinear; ends on the other segment in decimals binary cannot hold, also a kilometre out; an end 9 mm from the other's line beyond its end with the segments crossing; segments of no length; `IsSimplePolygon` and `Overlaps` rows in every rotation and direction of each ring), `FormulaPropertyTests` (the order property at `Math.Max(10_000, Iter)` cases, so 10,000 in every build, checked with a counting probe, over all eight orders; seed `cCcbgdLcNjA6` as a fixed case beside it, which runs exactly that input; an end placed on the other segment is a touch; a segment moved sideways touches within 1 cm and not beyond at any length; on a 10 cm grid the answer equals exact integer arithmetic; `IsSimplePolygon` and `Overlaps` the same in every rotation and direction of grid rings). Against the previous `Geometry.cs`, 9 of the new tests fail (the seed case and its row among them); with the fix all pass, and five runs at `ARIVA_FUZZ_ITERATIONS=20000` (100,000 cases per property) pass.
- Docs: formulas F4 (the track-crossing code uses F4's own side-of-line rule, not this predicate; the predicate described with its tolerance and canonical order), F22 (touching within 1 cm in the simple polygon rule), the property tests section; wiki 07 (polygon touches refused, footprint reach includes a touch); decisions 2026-10-12 entry and open decisions row.
- Gotchas: publication and `CreateDraft` do not re-check simplicity, so a stored zone with a vertex 1 to 9 mm beside another edge stays publishable until moved, and its export gives a bundle the import refuses (decisions point 7). Geometry.cs is not in Stryker's mutate list.

## 2026-10-12 ARV-156 Tests robust under load and on a busy broker (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Taken over after a container restart ended the first attempt before it reported; its uncommitted work was reviewed part by part. Kept: the start gate in `ArivaHosts.cs` (diagnosis verified against the sources; the build moved inside the `try`, so a failed build also opens the gate), `IsNamespaceName` and its table of names, the evidence files. Changed: the namespace rule (the first attempt's non-backtracking pattern plus an `EndsWith('-')` check became the original RFC 1123 pattern on `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` without a timeout) and its test. Dropped: `GeneratedRegexMatchers.cs`, which read the generated matcher's IL for calls to `RegexRunner.CheckTimeout` (it depends on how the generator emits its code and counts 0, a pass, should a later generator check the clock another way); the env-gated phase recorder in `BrokerOutageTests.cs`; `Arv156TemporaryReproTests.cs` (an env-gated repro, used for the load runs below and then removed).
- Cause 1, `ValidationReaderLoginTests` (Cronz), "Cannot access a disposed object. Object name: 'IServiceProvider'": a race in `WebApplicationFactory` with a host whose start fails, checked against the .NET 10 sources (aspnetcore v10.0.0 `DeferredHostBuilder.cs` and `WebApplicationFactory.cs`; runtime v10.0.0 `HostFactoryResolver.cs`, `Host.cs`, `HostingAbstractionsHostExtensions.cs`). The entry point runs on a thread of its own; `HostFactoryResolver` hands the built host to the factory at `HostBuilt` (`stopApplication: false`) and the entry point goes straight on into `app.RunAsync()`, whose `finally` disposes the host when `StartAsync` throws (here `ValidationReaderGuard`). The factory's thread meanwhile calls `DeferredHost.StartAsync`, which first resolves `IHostApplicationLifetime` from `_host.Services` and only then waits for the start's outcome. When the entry point's thread gets there first, the resolve meets the disposed provider: `ObjectDisposedException`, a subclass of `InvalidOperationException`, so only the test's message check failed. Any test whose host fails in its start rather than its build (a hosted service or a start-up validator refusing the configuration) had the same exposure.
- Fix 1 (test plumbing only, `Ariva.UnitTests/Setup/ArivaHosts.cs`): `GatedHostLifetime` wraps the host's `IHostLifetime` and holds `WaitForStartAsync` (the first step of `Host.StartAsync`, before the start-up validators and the hosted services) until a gate opens; `ArivaWebApplicationFactory.CreateHost` builds the host, calls the deferred host's `StartAsync` (which resolves the lifetime and subscribes before its first wait, so it returns at that wait), then opens the gate. A failed start is now always its own exception. No production host code changed. `HostStartGateTests` pins it deterministically: the start stays pending and no hosted service starts until the gate opens, and a booted host carries the gated lifetime.
- Proof 1 (16 `yes` CPU hogs on the 4 CPUs, started and stopped by PID): the first attempt's repro (four lanes of 500 refused starts each, Ingest, Stream, Cronz and Integration in k8s-dev with the reader login) before the fix, 20:17 to 20:21 UTC: 221 of 2,000 starts ended with `ObjectDisposedException` at `DeferredHost.StartAsync`, 1,779 with the guard's exception; after the fix, 20:47 to 20:51 UTC, with the whole integration suite also running: 2,000 of 2,000 the guard's exception. The two classes alone 50 times in a row before the fix (20:22 to 20:46 UTC): 50 passed (194 tests each), so the loop alone does not reproduce the race (200 refused starts, one at a time); after the fix (20:51 to 21:14 UTC, the hogs and the integration suite beside it, load average 20 to 29): 50 passed (217 tests each).
- Cause 2, `ValidationEmulatorTests.MainUrl_Should_BeTheAddressOfTheSimulatorsOwnDeployment_When_Checked`, `RegexMatchTimeoutException`: the simulator's namespace rule `^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?\z` had a 100 ms timeout on a backtracking matcher. A timeout is wall-clock time from the start of a match (`RegexRunner.InitializeTimeout`), compared only where the matcher calls `CheckTimeout`: the generated code does so where it backtracks (and the interpreter at every match), and this pattern backtracks on every name of two characters or more (the loop takes the last character, then gives it back). A thread descheduled or suspended for a garbage collection for 100 ms between the two fails a 9-character name: the input was not too long, the pattern backtracks. Measured under the 16 hogs plus 16 spinning threads and a large-object allocator, 30 s each against `"ariva-dev"`: the old matcher 14 timeouts in 1,733,996 matches (the slowest timed-out call 652 ms); the same pattern on `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` without a timeout 0 in 1,443,620 (its slowest call 2,664 ms, which any timeout would have failed).
- Fix 2 (`Ariva.Simulation.Api/Emulators/FeedSettings.cs`): the same RFC 1123 pattern with `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` and `Timeout.Infinite`. CWE-1333: the non-backtracking engine is linear in the input's length, which is the bound against ReDoS; without a timeout no match can throw `RegexMatchTimeoutException`. The rule and so `IsOwnDeploymentMain` (CWE-918) accept exactly the same names. Test: `NamespaceLabel_Should_BeLinearWithoutATimeout_When_Matched` (the options and the timeout, read from the rule itself) beside the table of names (`IsNamespaceName_Should_TakeAnRfc1123LabelOnly_When_Checked`, 21 cases, and the 63 and 64 character and 1,000,000 character cases). A test that the pattern has no nested quantifiers would not prove it: `^[a-z0-9-]{0,62}[a-z0-9]\z` has none and still backtracks.
- Proof 2: the loops of Proof 1 run `ValidationEmulatorTests` too (the MainUrl theory, 25 cases, 11 of them with an own namespace such as `ariva-dev`): 50 of 50 passed before the fix and 50 of 50 after, so the loops did not reproduce this one either; the matcher measurement above does (14 timeouts before, 0 after), and with no timeout on the rule there is nothing left to time out.
- Cause 3, `BrokerOutageTests.Outbox_Should_HoldEventsWhileTheBrokerIsDownAndRelayThemInOrder_When_ItIsBack`, timed out at 300 s. The cause found in round 1 is the test's own bound, not the broker, the outbox or a rebalance; the three timed out runs themselves were not reproduced (below). Revised in round 2: run 12's diagnosis (further down) gives a likelier cause, a cut during the consumer's offset commit. The test waited 90 s for readiness `Unhealthy` during the outage, but MassTransit reports the bus `Degraded` while its Kafka endpoint is faulted ("Degraded Endpoints: ariva-it.it-faults", every check from the cut to the restore in the host logs) and never `Unhealthy`, so that wait always ran its whole bound (90.2, 90.4, 90.4 and 90.4 s in the four instrumented runs) and then passed its `NotBe(Healthy)` assertion. With the direct publish's message timeout (30 to 38 s) about 125 s of the fact's 300 s were fixed cost; the rest had to cover the host's start (held by `KafkaTopicsReady` until the topics exist, up to 300 s by default, and not bounded by the test at all), the first three, the relay after the restore and the final check, whose own bounds (240, 60, 300 and 120 s) added up to 870 s, so a slow step could never fail with its name: the fact's timeout fired first, three times, with no trace of which step was slow. The other suspects, with evidence: no broker container restarts (the test disables the Toxiproxy proxy; the broker keeps running); the outbox relay holds every row while the bus is not healthy (`IOutboxTransport.IsReady`), so the rows written during the outage had 0 attempts and no backoff (one run had one attempt, a pass already producing when the cut came, with a 2 s backoff); after the restore the Kafka endpoint reconnects at MassTransit's next receive transport retry (exponential, 3 to 30 s, 1,000 tries, for every transport exception but a cancellation, each turned into a `KafkaConnectionException`: `InMemoryHostConfiguration`, `ReceiveTransport` and `TopicKafkaReceiveEndpointContext`, decompiled from MassTransit 8.5.11), rejoins its group and the relay sends at its next 200 ms poll: 20.6, 36.6, 27.2 and 27.9 s from the restore to all eight received.

- Diagnosis of run 34: a race in Testcontainers.Kafka 4.15.0's container start, not in the test or in Ariva. `KafkaBuilder` (decompiled; unchanged on the library's `develop` and `main` branches) starts the container with entrypoint `/bin/sh -c` and the command `while [ ! -f /testcontainers.sh ]; do sleep 0.1; done; /testcontainers.sh`, and its start callback copies the script in with `CopyAsync(..., "/testcontainers.sh", mode 755)` (a Docker archive upload). The loop sees the file as soon as it exists and executes it; when the copy still has it open for writing, `execve` fails with ETXTBSY ("Text file busy"), the shell exits 126, and the container stops before Kafka starts. A loaded machine widens that window. Every Kafka fixture of the integration suite starts its container the same way, so any of them can fail like this in a gate. Proposed, not applied (stop and report): give the fixtures' Kafka containers a command that never executes a file that may still be written, `while [ ! -s /testcontainers.sh ]; do sleep 0.1; done; /bin/sh /testcontainers.sh` (the shell reads the script instead of executing it, and waits for it to be non-empty; the script is a few hundred bytes written in one piece), in one shared builder used by `FaultsFixture` and the other Kafka fixtures, and report the race to Testcontainers; then the gates and the 50-run loop again.

In Testcontainers 4.15.0 `WithCommand(params string[])` appends to the module's command, so the builder replaces it with `OverwriteEnumerable`. Every place the suite builds a Kafka container (a search for `KafkaBuilder`, `KafkaContainer`, `ContainerBuilder(`, `cp-kafka` and `apache/kafka` in Platform): `Messaging/KafkaPipelineTests.cs` (`KafkaFixture`, used by `KafkaPipelineTests`, `TopicProvisioningTests`, `AmanKafkaTests`, `QueueStreamTests`, `QueueStreamScaleOutTests` and `QueueStreamEventTimeTests`) and `Faults/FaultsFixture.cs`; both now use the builder. Not Testcontainers.Kafka, so not affected: `DatabaseChartBootstrapTests` (a database image), the Aspire AppHost (`AddKafka`), the CI and ZAP service containers and `docker-compose.dev.yml` (`apache/kafka:4.1.0`), and the E2E services script. Checked: `docker inspect` of both fixtures' containers during a run shows entrypoint `["/bin/sh","-c"]` and the new command, and `BrokerOutageTests` with `TopicProvisioningTests` passed (2 of 2).
- Ready-to-paste issue for Testcontainers (the owner's call to file; not filed). Title: "Kafka module: container exits 126 'Text file busy' when the start script is executed while it is still being copied". Version: Testcontainers.Kafka 4.15.0 (.NET; the same command on the `develop` and `main` branches), Docker on Linux, image `confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.1`. The start command: `KafkaBuilder.Init()` sets the entrypoint `/bin/sh -c` and the command `while [ ! -f /testcontainers.sh ]; do sleep 0.1; done; /testcontainers.sh`, and the start callback copies the script in with `CopyAsync(..., "/testcontainers.sh", fileMode: Unix.FileMode755)`. The race: the loop sees the file as soon as it exists and executes it; if the archive copy still holds it open for writing, `execve` fails with ETXTBSY, the container log shows "/bin/sh: /testcontainers.sh: Text file busy", the shell exits 126 and `StartAsync` throws `ContainerNotRunningException` ("exited with code 126"). Reproduction hint: start many Kafka containers in a loop on a loaded host (we saw it once in about 34 fixture starts beside 16 CPU-bound processes on 4 CPUs). Workaround: replace the command, `.WithCommand(new OverwriteEnumerable<string>(["while [ ! -s /testcontainers.sh ]; do sleep 0.1; done; /bin/sh /testcontainers.sh"]))`, so the shell reads the script instead of executing a file that may still be open for writing; a fix in the module could copy the script under another name and rename it into place, or use the same `/bin/sh` form.

## 2026-10-13 ARV-166 A produce queued behind an in-flight message on a dropped connection never completes (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Started on 5bf7106 (tree clean). Passes true after the security review. Findings are written here as they come (the container has restarted twice recently).
- Cause (found 2026-10-13, 07:40 to 08:08 UTC; a temporary diagnostic test against the faults fixture, kept out of the tree, with the ARV-156 sequence: warm-up, `FaultsFixture.StallAsync`, produce A not awaited, `CutAsync` 2 s later, produce B 0.5 s after that, `RestoreAsync`, produce C): not librdkafka, not idempotence, not `message.timeout.ms`: MassTransit 8.5.11's rider destroys the producer that B is waiting on. (1) A plain Confluent.Kafka 2.15.1 producer with Ariva's own settings (`KafkaClientConfig.Producer`: idempotence, `Acks.All`, `MessageTimeoutMs` 30,000, `LingerMs` 0), never disposed: A ended "Local: Message timed out" after 38.8 s and B after 36.3 s, reported together (librdkafka debug: "timed out 2+0 message(s) (MsgId 2..3): message.timeout.ms exceeded", then the idempotent epoch-bump drain); C succeeded after the restore. So librdkafka reports a message queued behind one in flight on a dropped connection. (2) The same producer disposed 5 s after B (as below, no flush): A and B never completed, still pending 150 s after the dispose and 60 s after the restore. (3) Through `ISvcMessageBus` (MassTransit), twice: A ended after 30.9 s and 31.8 s; B was pending 90 s after the cut and 45 s after the restore; C succeeded in 0.5 s; the producer that had logged "Error (Local_AllBrokersDown) ... on producer: ariva-diag166#producer-4" every 2 to 10 s logged nothing after A's S-FAULT, and a cut after C was reported by `#producer-11`: a new librdkafka instance. The chain, read in the decompiled 8.5.11 assemblies: `KafkaTopicSendTransportContext.Send` runs the produce inside `PipeContextSupervisor<ProducerContext>.Send`, which on any exception from the pipe (a delivery failure, a local error, or a cancellation) calls `activeContext.Faulted`; `ActivePipeContext.Faulted` disposes the shared, cached producer context ("recreated whenever a fault is propagated to the usage"); `KafkaProducerContext.Dispose` flushes with a token linked to a source that its `OnError` handler cancelled at the first local error (here `Local_AllBrokersDown` at the cut), so the flush ends at once, and then disposes the Confluent producer; `Producer.Dispose` stops its poll thread and destroys the handle, and librdkafka silently discards outstanding messages on destroy (rdkafka.h: "you should call rd_kafka_flush() before you destroy the producer. Otherwise, any outstanding messages will be silently discarded"). B's delivery handler is never invoked, so its `TaskCompletionSource` never completes, and its `GCHandle` (with the key and value) is never freed. One producer per topic (the rider keeps one per registered topic), so any failed or cancelled produce on a topic strands every other produce outstanding on that topic at that moment, broker outage or not: a device push whose request is aborted cancels its produce and strands the other pushes on the same topic. In run 16 the relay's row 4 and the direct publish shared `ariva.sla.breach-detected.v1`. The librdkafka 2.15.1 and 2.16.0 changelogs and the Confluent.Kafka 2.16.0 changelog list nothing about undelivered reports; 2.16.0 reports `ALL_BROKERS_DOWN` once per outage instead of every re-bootstrap, which does not change the chain (one local error is enough).
- Why the ARV-156 timing reproduces only sometimes (found 2026-10-13 08:31 UTC): a message that has been sent is timed out by the broker's own thread, which scans its queue only when it wakes, and while the broker is unreachable it wakes at each reconnect attempt (librdkafka's `reconnect.backoff.max.ms`, 10 s). When the scan that times out the first message also catches the one queued behind it (both due within the same wake-up), both reports arrive before the rider disposes the producer and nothing is stranded: the new test with the ARV-156 timing (B 0.5 s after the cut) passed once on the unfixed code, the row, A and B all reported together 9 s after the row was due. In the two diagnostic runs through MassTransit the wake-ups (every 10 s, visible in the producer's "Local_AllBrokersDown" lines at 13.8, 23.8 and 33.8 s) fell between A's and B's deadlines, so B was stranded. Queuing B more than 10 s after the first message makes the strand certain: B is due after the first message's latest possible report. The test does that (B 12 s after the cut).
- Mechanism chosen (and why): the cause sits in MassTransit's rider, which Ariva cannot change, and the cause-level fix (one Ariva-owned Confluent producer per host for produces, the rider kept for consumers; never disposed on a failed send) would replace the implementation behind `ISvcMessageBus` and so contradict CLAUDE.md's messaging rule and ADR-0018's decision 1; it is recorded as an open decision for the owner (`docs/product/decisions.md`, ADR-0018 note of 2026-10-13). Within the rider: (1) `KafkaProduce` bounds every produce Ariva awaits (`SendTimeout` 45 s: librdkafka's 30 s message timeout, its reporting delay of up to the 10 s reconnect backoff, measured 30.6 to 39.5 s in ARV-156 and 36.3 to 39.1 s here, plus 5 s): the produce gets a token of its own that cancels at the bound (Confluent completes its await as cancelled, the rider releases it), and the wait itself ends at the bound (`WaitAsync`) even if a client ignores the token; a produce that runs out fails with `KafkaProduceTimeoutException` (a `TimeoutException`, so Ingest answers 503 and the relay ends its pass). (2) The caller's token never reaches the rider: before, a device dropping its request cancelled its produce, which made the rider dispose the topic's producer and strand every other push on that topic; now the caller stops waiting at once and its produce runs on to its report or its bound, observed in a continuation. (3) The relay's pass produces for at most `Kafka:Outbox:PassSeconds` (60 s): each send is awaited for what is left of it (a token and `WaitAsync`), and one that runs out is a broker failure (row failed with its backoff, key held back, pass committed). (4) The dead-letter retry loops (`DeadLetterFilter`, `UnreadableFilter`, through `DeadLetterRetry`) end on `MessagingShutdown`, signalled by `ApplicationStopping` and by the bus's `PreStop` (an `IBusObserver`, which also covers a host disposed without a stop, the ARV-156 case); the stream worker's dead-letter loop and `PartitionedConsumer` now take the worker's token instead of `CancellationToken.None`. (5) `dotnet.producer.delivery.report.fields` none: a stranded delivery handler stays pinned by its GCHandle for good, and without the key, value and headers it costs a few hundred bytes instead of up to 1 MB. No librdkafka setting changes the behaviour (the producer is destroyed; no setting stops the rider from doing that), so none was changed beyond (5).
- Cause verified by a second reading (2026-10-13, after the restart; ilspycmd on the net10.0 assemblies of MassTransit 8.5.11, MassTransit.Kafka 8.5.11 and Confluent.Kafka 2.15.1 in the NuGet cache). The caller's token reaches librdkafka's await: `TopicProducer<TKey,TValue>.Produce(key, value, pipe, cancellationToken)` passes it to `KafkaTopicSendTransportContext.Send(IPipe<ProducerContext>, cancellationToken)` and into `SendPipe`, whose `CreateContext` builds `KafkaMessageSendContext` with it, and `KafkaTopicSendTransportContext.Send(ProducerContext, KafkaSendContext)` calls `producerContext.Produce(topic, message, sendContext.CancellationToken)`, which is Confluent's `Producer.ProduceAsync`; there `cancellationToken.Register(() => handler.TrySetCanceled())` completes the await as cancelled and leaves the message queued in librdkafka. The cancellation then faults the shared producer: `PipeContextSupervisor<TContext>.Send` has `catch (Exception exception) { await activeContext.Faulted(exception); throw; }` with no filter, so an `OperationCanceledException` is a fault like any other; `ProducerContextFactory.CreateActiveContext` gives `SupervisorExtensions.AddActiveContext(supervisor, contextHandle, ...)`, an `ActivePipeContext<T>` over the cached handle, and `ActivePipeContext<T>.Faulted` is `await _contextHandle.DisposeAsync()`; the handle is the `AsyncPipeContextAgent<ProducerContext>` from `GetContext`, whose `DisposeAsync` is `PipeContextAgent<T>.DisposeAsync` (first call only: `_inactive.TrySetResult`), which disposes the `KafkaProducerContext`, and `GetContext` creates a new producer on the next send because the handle `IsDisposed`. `KafkaProducerContext.Dispose` flushes with a 30 s token linked to `_cancellationTokenSource`, which `OnError` cancels at the first local error (`error.IsLocalError`: a broker down, but also an idle disconnect reported as `Local_Transport`), so on such a producer the flush ends at once; then `Producer.Dispose` cancels the poll task (`callbackCts.Cancel(); callbackTask.Wait()`) and disposes the handle: no delivery report is served after that, so the `TypedTaskDeliveryHandlerShim` of every message still outstanding never completes (its `GCHandle` stays). Finding (2) holds: a caller's cancellation disposes the shared producer. Two details the first reading did not record: on a producer that has never seen a local error the dispose flushes for up to 30 s synchronously on the faulting send's thread (outstanding messages then get their reports, nothing is stranded); and a second fault on an already disposed handle is a no-op (`TrySetResult` false), so a stranded produce cancelled at Ariva's 45 s bound does not dispose the producer that replaced it. Ariva's own bound does cancel through the same path: when the 45 s token fires on a producer that is still live (librdkafka not having reported by then, which the measurements make rare: 30.6 to 39.5 s), that producer is disposed too; accepted, because every send stranded by it is bounded the same way. The token is what releases a stranded produce's async chain (rider and Confluent state machines, which hold the serialised message); `dotnet.producer.delivery.report.fields` none then leaves the pinned handler without the key and value, so (1) and (5) belong together.
- The uncommitted DeadLetterShutdownTests failed before the restart (scratchpad 166/after, 08:48 to 08:59: both cases, "the poison message delivered again and dead-lettered after the restart" not within 270 s). Cause, from its host log and the decompiled pipes: the loop's `OperationCanceledException` carried the linked token, not the message's, so MassTransit's `RetryFilter<TContext>` (it rethrows only when `ex.CancellationToken` is the context's) treated it as a failure and retried; with `RetryCount` 0 `ExponentialRetryPolicy.GetRetryInterval` threw `IndexOutOfRangeException` (R-RETRY then R-FAULT in the log), which the receive pipe's `RescueFilter` (configured by `ReceivePipeConfiguration.CreatePipe` with `Ignore<OperationCanceledException>()` only) sent to the error pipe, so the message completed and its offset was committed: lost, neither dead-lettered nor redelivered. An `OperationCanceledException` that escapes the pipe instead is not rescued: `ReceivePipeDispatcher.Dispatch` calls `receiveLock.Faulted`, and `KafkaReceiveLockContext` marks the offset's `PendingConfirmation` faulted, so it is not committed by itself. Fix: the loop ends with an `OperationCanceledException` that carries the message's own token.
- Proven with a temporary revert (the loop ending with its linked token again; `ConsumePipelineTests.Pipe_Should_LeaveTheMessageUnacknowledgedWithoutRetryOrFault_When_TheEndpointStopsWhileItsDeadLetterIsRefused` and the three `BoundedProduceTests` that check the token, 5 of 5 failed, then the fix restored): with `RetryCount` 0 the receive ended in `IndexOutOfRangeException` and a published `Fault<T>` (rescued: acknowledged, the message lost); with `RetryCount` 2 the receive did end as a cancellation (not acknowledged) but the retry filter's exhausted path (`RetryFaulted`, `NotifyPendingFaults`) published a `Fault<T>`. So the production default (3) kept the message but published a spurious fault, and a host configured without retries lost it. Residual, not fixable inside the rider: MassTransit's `BatchCheckpointer.ReadBatch` awaits each `PendingConfirmation` in offset order and, when one is faulted, checkpoints the ones before it and carries on, so a later record of the same partition (another key; `ConcurrentMessageLimit` 8) that completes and is checkpointed (every `CheckpointInterval`, 5 s) before `KafkaMessageConsumer.ActiveAndActualAgentsCompleted` cancels the checkpoint token commits past the record left unacknowledged at the stop. It needs the broker to take commits while refusing the dead letter (a partial outage, not a full one: then the commit fails too); the stop warning now names topic, partition and offset so that the record can be replayed. Before ARV-166 the same message kept the pod from stopping until it was killed, which kept it.
- Changes by the second engineer (2026-10-13, after the restart): (a) `DeadLetterRetry.SendUntilAcceptedAsync` takes the message's token and the stop token apart and always ends with an `OperationCanceledException` carrying the message's token; its two log lines name the partition (also the stream worker's), for a replay. (b) `OutboxRelay.SendWithinAsync` waits on the same linked token it gives the transport (`WaitAsync(linked.Token)`) instead of a second timer: with two timers due at the same moment the row's error was sometimes "The operation has timed out." (seen in a StuckProduceTests host log) instead of naming the pass bound. (c) StuckProduceTests: the host runs with `Kafka:Outbox:PassSeconds` 20, so the relay's pass is ended by its own bound against the real stuck produce (measured 20.2 s), checked from the committed row without a lock (the bus stayed Healthy through the cut, so the relay ran passes back to back, 09:26:00 to :20 and :20 to :40 in the host log, and a later pass relocked the row), and the leader lock is polled every 25 ms to catch the 200 ms gap between passes; new fact `Produce_Should_NotStrandTheOtherSends_When_ACallerGivesUp` (stall, a send outstanding, cut, wait for the producer's `Local_AllBrokersDown`, another caller gives up, restore): first run, the outstanding send completed after 11.2 s and both messages were consumed once, in order. (d) ConsumePipelineTests and BoundedProduceTests as above, plus a test that an abandoned produce's later failure raises no unobserved task exception (with a control that does). (e) BrokerOutageTests: the comments now say the race is bounded, not removed (ARV-167). (f) Docs: ADR-0018 note rewritten before commit and the owner's decision added (ARV-167); decisions.md records the owner's decision (the open row removed); overview, cwe-controls (CWE-400), asvs-l2 and wiki 10 corrected (the dead-letter stop, the checkpoint residual, which ARV-167 does not change, and what operators see).
- Found 2026-10-13 09:40 (DeadLetterShutdownTests with MassTransit at Debug, scratchpad 166/diag3): with the loop ending as the message's cancellation the record is no longer acknowledged (T-FAULT instead of R-FAULT, and offset 6 did come back), but the test still failed: a consumer of the first host, created after that host's bus had stopped and its provider was disposed, took the partition at the next rebalance and faulted the record on every assignment ("ObjectDisposedException: IServiceProvider" from `RiderRegistrationContext.GetService`, then the stop warning, since that host's `MessagingShutdown` was cancelled), so the restarted host never got it. Mechanism, read in MassTransit 8.5.11: at the cut `KafkaMessageConsumer.HandleKafkaError` cancels the consume loop on any local error ("Consume Loop Exited" at 09:40:38.765); the consumer completes only when its dispatch ends; `MessagingShutdown` (ApplicationStopping, or the bus's PreStop) ended the dispatch before the bus stop chose its endpoints, so the endpoint reported Completed ("Endpoint Completed" at 09:40:41.98) and `ReceiveEndpointCollection.StopEndpoints` skips it (it stops only endpoints whose `IsStarted()`: Started, Ready or Faulted), its `ReceiveTransportAgent` is never stopped, and its `Run` loop starts the transport again after its one second delay: a new Confluent consumer at 09:40:42.998, after "Bus stopped" at 09:40:42.17. Fix: the loops end on their own endpoint's `IReceiveEndpointObserver.Stopping`, which `ReceiveEndpoint.Stop` raises after the endpoint was chosen and before `TransportHandle.Stop`, so the transport agent is stopping before the dispatch can end and nothing restarts. `MessagingShutdown` (host lifetime and bus observer) is replaced by a per-endpoint signal connected in `ConsumePipeline.Configure`. Independent of ARV-166 and left as found: a Kafka endpoint whose consumer ended on a broker error and is between restarts when the bus stops is skipped the same way and restarts into a stopped host; in production the process exits right after the stop, so it lasts until then (the group then waits out the member's session).
- Verified on the real broker (2026-10-13 10:08, scratchpad 166/neg): `StuckProduceTests.Produce_Should_NotStrandTheOtherSends_When_ACallerGivesUp` with the caller's token linked into the produce again (a temporary build, source restored): the send outstanding when another caller gave up ended only at the bound, "after 45.0 s (KafkaProduceTimeoutException)", although the broker was back 2 s after the caller gave up; with the fix it completed after 11.0 s and both messages were consumed. This is finding (2) observed end to end: a caller's cancellation disposes the producer the other sends are on. DeadLetterShutdownTests (both cases) passed after the endpoint signal and a fix to the test's dead-letter reader (it stopped at its first empty 500 ms poll, which a fresh consumer's first fetch can exceed): the poison message was delivered again and dead-lettered after the restart at 51.5 s and 47.1 s (the restarted host waits out the old member's session, about 36 s, since the old host closed its consumer while the broker was still cut).
- Found while answering whether (2) keeps at-least-once (2026-10-13, read in `ZoneProcessor` and `QueueStateEngine.Interval`): nothing is lost (an abandoned produce runs on to its report or bound, and the device resends a push whose request it dropped, with the same batch id), but the duplicate is not dropped everywhere. The sensing archive drops it (`sensing_batch`), consumers behind the inbox drop theirs by event id, and the queue engine counts a repeated track entry or exit as a duplicate; it has no batch-id check, though, so a repeated interval-count batch is applied again (`Interval` tallies `In` and `Out` again). Pre-existing for any resend whose first produce reached the broker (docs/architecture/sensor-adapters.md says consumers drop a resent body, which holds for the archive, not for the engine), and more frequent with (2), since an abandoned produce now completes. Not fixed here: the coordinator made it ARV-168 (priority 37); the overview (Producing) and the ADR-0018 note point to it.
- Gates (2026-10-13, on fresh services, the tree as handed back): `node scripts/verify.mjs backend` exit 0 (PASS dotnet build, golden, unit tests, scanner self-test, security scan, base images, chart security, NuGet and npm audits); `node scripts/verify.mjs story --specs tests/api/device-push.spec.ts,tests/api/device-health.spec.ts,tests/api/aman-feed.spec.ts --integration "FullyQualifiedName~BrokerOutage|...|FullyQualifiedName~QueueStream"` exit 0, widened to the full suites (wide: Ariva.Infra Messaging and Streaming): unit 5,242 passed, integration 513 passed and 1 skipped, E2E 687 passed and 1 skipped; `node scripts/security/scan.mjs --changed` exit 0 (16 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings); `node scripts/verify.mjs docs` exit 0. The coordinator recorded the owner's decision in decisions.md (2026-10-13, point 1) and made the repeated interval-count batch ARV-168; this entry's decisions bullet refers to it.
- Tallies after the gates (2026-10-13 10:51 to 11:32, one process per run, 16 `yes` hogs, stopped afterwards): StuckProduceTests 10 of 10 passed (both facts each run, 121 to 128 s a run); BrokerOutageTests 10 of 10 passed (110 to 134 s). Passes stays false, until the security review.
- Security review (security-reviewer; CWE-400, with CWE-532 and at-least-once): PASS (2026-10-13) on code, tests and docs: every awaited produce goes through BoundedAsync; the relay cannot hold its transaction, lock or rows past PassSeconds; Ingest answers 503 with Retry-After within the bound; the dead-letter loops end at a stop without acknowledging; nothing of a message is logged. `scan.mjs --changed` 16 files, 0 errors. Conditions met by the lead: C1, residual (a) is new reachability made by this change (before it the stop hung and nothing was lost), so the owner decided on 2026-10-13 to accept it for ARV-166 and close it before the pilot in ARV-171 (a refused dead letter written durably first); C2, ADR-0018's note now says so. Also: residual (b), the stray consumer, folded into ARV-165; the producer queue bound for ARV-167; the review's test recommendations in ARV-171; the 'Decided' cells in decisions.md punctuated.

## 2026-10-13 ARV-168 The queue engine drops a resent interval-count batch (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Started on 8837801 (tree clean). Passes true after the security review. Findings are written here as they come.
- How a batch id travels (traced 2026-10-13 11:50 UTC): the device sends no batch id of its own. Ingest (`SensingIngest.IngestAsync`) maps one push into at most one batch per kind (tracks, crossings, occupancy, intervals) and stamps each batch's `EventBase.Id` with `BatchId(device id, kind, SHA-256 of the body[, receipt ticks for receipt-timed kinds])`, a version 8 GUID, so the same body from the same device repeats the id and anything else gets a new one. The vendor's package id (`packageId`, Xovis `package_info.id`, a declarative `package` path) is only `SensingBatch.PackageId`, a `long?` copied from the first package, used for nothing in the engine. The id is on the batch envelope only: the events inside (`Sensed<IntervalCount>` and the others) carry none. It reaches Kafka as the record's JSON `id` (keyed by the zone key) and the Stream worker reads it back with the batch (`QueueStreamWorker.Read`). The archive stores it per row (`sensing_event.batch_id`) and drops a repeat by id alone within three days (`sensing_batch`); `ArchivedBatch.ToBatch` gives it back to a replay. Health reports have random version 7 ids and never repeat. Device-supplied data reaches the id only through the body hash: a device cannot choose another device's id, since the device id is part of the hash.
- The defect confirmed by reading: `ZoneProcessor.Offer` maps every batch to engine inputs with no look at `batch.Id`; a repeat whose events are still ahead of the watermark is buffered and applied again (`QueueStateEngine.Interval` tallies In and Out a second time; an anonymous vendor crossing, track id null, is counted again too). Tracked crossings are protected by the track rule (first entry counts: `_byTrack` and the 20,000 `_resolvedTracks`), occupancy and track samples repeat harmlessly (same reading again), desk zone readings are dropped by `DeskZoneReadings` (a time not after the last one is superseded).
- Found while writing the unit tests (2026-10-13 12:00 UTC, a temporary probe test, removed): a separate, pre-existing quirk of `QueueStateEngine.Interval`, not fixed here. Two interval readings that end at the same instant (the entry line's and the exit line's counts of one T1 push, or two devices counting one line) are applied one after the other, and after the first the engine's cursor is at that instant, so the second is spread over nothing: all its people land at the interval's end, which is the next minute. One push of minute 17:03 (5 in on the entry line, 3 out on the exit line) gives `line_minute` entry 17:03 in 5 and exit 17:04 out 3, and zone minutes 17:03 entries 5, 17:04 exits 3. ARV-148's point (4) mended the same effect for an occupancy reading of the instant applied first, not for a second interval. It shifts the later line's counts (by line name) by one minute for T1 devices; totals are right. Changing it may change the golden replay if the reference evening has such pushes, so it is for the coordinator (a story of its own). The ARV-168 tests therefore check the evening's totals and the entry line's minute, never the exit line's minute.
- Built (2026-10-13, 12:00 to 12:15 UTC): `RecentBatches` in Ariva.Core/Queueing (pure) and `ZoneProcessor` remembers each batch of a device with a non-empty id, key (device code, batch id), until the watermark reaches its latest event time (events within the engine's MaxAhead of the batch's receive time) plus the lateness; a batch already remembered is dropped before its events reach any engine (counter `RepeatedBatches`), after `Heard` and the receive clock, so it is exactly a health report at its receive time. ## 2026-10-13 ARV-172 BoundedProduceTests deadline race under load (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Started on d055ec0 (tree clean). Passes true after the security review. Findings are written here as they come.
- Cause confirmed by reading (13:50 UTC): `KafkaProduce.BoundedAsync` starts two independent timers with the same bound, the produce's own `CancellationTokenSource(bound, time)` and `send.WaitAsync(bound, time, ct)`, and nothing orders them. On Linux the runtime's timer thread does not run callbacks itself: it hands each due timer queue to the thread pool, where the first due timer in the queue's list runs on that pool thread and every other due timer is queued as a work item of its own (and a newer timer is linked ahead of an older one), so when both are due together the wait's timer tends to run first while the deadline's callback waits for a pool thread. The wait then fails with `TimeoutException`, mapped to `KafkaProduceTimeoutException`, and the test reads `given.IsCancellationRequested` before the deadline's callback has run. When the deadline's timer runs first, the produce's `Task.Delay(Infinite, token)` cancels and the same exception surfaces through the `OperationCanceledException` path, the token already cancelled. Either way the caller sees the same exception and the token is cancelled at the bound: the code is correct and the test races.
- Before the fix, the test alone beside 16 hogs (`yes > /dev/null`, 16 on 4 CPUs; 13:56 to 14:04 UTC, one test per process through the xUnit v3 executable, `--filter-method`): 50 of 50 passed, so the hogs alone do not reproduce it in a process that runs nothing else; the gates' failures came from the full unit suite, whose thread pool is busy.
- Confirmed by a probe (14:05 to 14:10 UTC; a scratch console app outside the tree that calls the real `BoundedAsync` by reflection with the test's produce delegate and reads the token the moment the timeout reaches the caller): alone and sequential, the wait's timer ran first in 99 of 100 calls and the token was not yet cancelled in 12 of them; 64 calls in parallel, 73 of 1,000 not yet cancelled. Beside 16 hogs: sequential, 86 of 100 not yet cancelled; 64 in parallel, 183 of 1,000. Every one of those tokens was cancelled after it, within 100 ms (most under 1 ms; at most 10 to 100 ms, 5 cases, beside the hogs and in parallel), never missed. The test passes alone only because FluentAssertions' exception chain usually takes longer than the deadline's callback.
- Before the fix, the full unit suite beside 16 hogs (old build; 14:07 to 14:26 UTC): 5,286 of 5,286 passed in 19.5 min, so one full run did not reproduce it either; the two further runs planned were stopped (about 20 min each, and the rebuild needed their binaries).
- Reproduced in one process (14:27 to 14:29 UTC; a second scratch console app outside the tree runs the test's own FluentAssertions 6.12 chain, before and after this story, against the real `BoundedAsync` by reflection, many at a time): alone, 64 in parallel, the old chain failed 109 of 1,000 with the gates' message ("Expected given.IsCancellationRequested to be true because the produce's own token cancels at the bound, so the client lets go of it, but found False."), the new chain passed 1,000 of 1,000. Beside 16 hogs: old 336 of 2,000 failed (64 in parallel) and 85 of 100 (sequential); new 2,000 of 2,000 and 100 of 100 passed.
- Fix (test only, production code unchanged): `Produce_Should_CancelItsOwnTokenAndFailAsATimeout_When_TheBoundPasses` registers on the produce's token a `TaskCompletionSource` (continuations asynchronous) that the cancellation completes, and after the `KafkaProduceTimeoutException` awaits it with FluentAssertions' `CompleteWithinAsync(10 s)`: a bounded condition, no fixed sleep, and it still fails if the token is never cancelled. The exception assertion (a `KafkaProduceTimeoutException`, not an `OperationCanceledException`) is unchanged.
- No ordering defect: whichever timer runs first, the caller gets the same `KafkaProduceTimeoutException` and the token is cancelled at the bound (within 100 ms after the caller, measured under the heaviest load). No caller acts on the produce or its producer in that window: Ingest answers 503, the relay bounds its pass with its own single linked token, the dead-letter retry backs off for 2 s or more. A strict order would need one timer for both, as `OutboxRelay.SendWithinAsync` already does ("One timer decides both"); proposed, not made.
- Same pattern, other tests (read 14:00 UTC): in BoundedProduceTests, `Produce_Should_Complete_When_TheBrokerAcknowledges` assumed that a 10 ms `Task.Delay` acknowledgement reaches the wait before the 300 ms bound's timers run, the same timer ordering assumption with a 290 ms margin; never seen to fail (0 of 3,000 probe calls, alone and beside 16 hogs), fixed anyway so the file holds no timer race: the test now gives the acknowledgement itself while the produce is waited for (asserting it is still waiting), with a 30 s bound. Checked and not affected: the other facts in BoundedProduceTests (the never-reporting produce ignores its token, so only the wait's timer can end it; the caller and dead-letter tests end by cancellation, not by a timer; `DeadLetter_Should_RetryUntilAccepted` has a 2 s backoff under a 10 s bound, a plain safety bound), StuckProduceTests (both paths give the same exception, which is all it asserts; the relay's 20 s pass bound against the 45 s produce bound is 25 s apart) and OutboxRelayTests' `Relay_Should_EndThePassWithinItsBoundAndLetGo_When_ASendNeverEnds` (`SendWithinAsync` uses one timer for the send's token and the wait).
- After the fix (rebuilt 14:30 UTC), beside 16 hogs (14:31 to 14:38 UTC): both changed facts, `Produce_Should_CancelItsOwnTokenAndFailAsATimeout_When_TheBoundPasses` and `Produce_Should_Complete_When_TheBrokerAcknowledges`, in one process per run through the xUnit v3 executable: 50 of 50 runs in a row passed, 2 of 2 tests each; the hogs stopped afterwards. The whole BoundedProduceTests class alone: 11 of 11.
- Gates (fresh services, detached; 14:38 to 14:45 UTC): `node scripts/verify.mjs backend` exit 0: PASS dotnet build, reference scenario golden up to date, unit tests (5,286 of 5,286, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 4 m 18 s), security scanner self-test, security scan (1,305 files, 0 errors, 6 warnings), base images pinned, chart security, NuGet vulnerability audit, npm audits (web, e2e). `node scripts/security/scan.mjs --changed` exit 0 (1 file, 0 errors, 0 warnings). `node scripts/verify.mjs docs` exit 0 (PASS docs text rules). Security review pending; the story stays passes false until it is recorded here.
- Security review (security-reviewer; test determinism, correctness judged): PASS (2026-10-13). The timeout test still requires the produce's own token to cancel and the call to fail as a timeout, and cannot pass if the token never cancels; the race is not a production defect (the order of two events within about 100 ms changes, not the outcome: Ingest's 503, the relay's own single timer, the duplicate dropped by the inbox, archive or engine); the second test's change is in scope. `scan.mjs --changed` 1 file, 0 errors. Both recommendations go to ARV-167, which replaces this send path: one timer for the produce's token and the wait, and the timeout test asserting the cancellation lands between the bound and the bound plus 5 s.

## 2026-10-13 ARV-171 A dead letter refused at a stop is kept durably, so no record is skipped (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Started on a3b8dfb (tree clean). Passes false until the security review. Closes ARV-166's residual (a) (review condition C1): a record faulted at a stop because Kafka refused its dead letter can be committed past by a later record of its partition. Findings are written here as they come.
- Design facts (read 2026-10-13): `outbox_message` (script 0011) fits a dead letter as it is: `topic varchar(120)` with `CHECK (topic ~ '^(ariva|aman)\.[a-z0-9.-]+$')` (a dead-letter topic `ariva.<...>.v1.dlq.v1` matches), `message_key varchar(200)` with a length check (a record's key can be longer or empty, so the row key needs a bound), `payload jsonb`, `headers jsonb`, unique `id`. `KafkaTopics.DeadLetter(topic)` throws for a topic that is not a constant, so the row's topic is never built from input. The relay can be led by any host, but each host registers dead-letter producers only for the topics it consumes, and for an unregistered topic MassTransit 8.5.11 makes a default producer (`KafkaFactoryConfigurator.CreateSendTransportContext` falls back to `CreateSpecification`, without Ariva's JSON value serializer), so every host must register the dead-letter producer of every known topic before a dead letter can go through the outbox. The relay's transport resolves a row's type through `EventCatalog`, which knows events only, so a dead-letter row needs its own type name there.
- Plan (2026-10-13): (1) `DeadLetterRetry`, when the loop ends without Kafka taking the letter (the endpoint stopping or the message's token), first writes the letter as an `outbox_message` row through a new `IDeadLetterStore` (`OutboxDeadLetterStore`: its own connection and short transaction, bounded in time, `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` on an id derived from consumer, topic, partition and offset, so a redelivered record adds no second row), then returns so the record completes; only when that write fails (the database away, its bound, a disposed host) does it end as ARV-166's cancellation of the message's token. (2) Message type `ariva.dead-letter`, a name no event class can have; the relay's transport deserialises it as `DeadLetter`, checks that the row's topic is `KafkaTopics.DeadLetter(letter.Topic)` of a known topic, and produces it through `KafkaProduce` as the direct sink does. (3) Every host registers the dead-letter producer of every topic in `KafkaTopics.All` (the topic provisioner already creates all of them), so any relay leader can send any dead letter in Ariva's JSON. (4) `DeadLetters.Create` guarantees that the letter's JSON fits Kafka's limit less 16 KB (EventCatalog's encoder escapes non-ASCII as six bytes, so 50 long headers could pass 1 MB today): the body gives way first, then the headers. (5) Row key: the record's key when it fits `message_key`, `none` when empty, else `sha256-<hex>` (the letter keeps the full key). Test plan: refuse only the dead-letter topic with a topic config, `max.message.bytes` 1 (the broker answers MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE at once, commits and every other topic unaffected; Toxiproxy cuts the whole connection, so it cannot refuse one topic), then delete the override to restore.
- Built (2026-10-13): `DeadLetters` (`MaxLetterBytes`, `OutboxMessageType` `ariva.dead-letter`, `IdOf`, `OutboxKeyOf`, the fit in `Create`), `IDeadLetterStore` and `OutboxDeadLetterStore` (Npgsql, own connection, parameterised constant SQL, `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING`), `DeadLetterRetry` keeps the letter within `KeepTimeout` (10 s) before faulting, both filters and `ConsumePipeline` pass the store, `MassTransitOutboxTransport.SendDeadLetterAsync` (row topic must equal `KafkaTopics.DeadLetter(letter.Topic)` of a known topic), every host registers the dead-letter producers of `KafkaTopics.All` and the store. Builds clean; tests next.
- Found (2026-10-13, the ARV-166 review's retry-wait case): a stop does not cancel a retry wait. `ConsumePipeline` calls `UseMessageRetry` on the endpoint (`IConsumePipeConfigurator`), whose MassTransit 8.5.11 overload builds `MessageRetryConfigurationObserver(configurator, CancellationToken.None, ...)` (only the overload that takes an `IBusFactoryConfigurator` connects a `RetryBusObserver` and cancels at the bus's stop). So the stop waits out the retry schedule, the remaining attempts run, and the final attempt dead-letters the message (or keeps it, ARV-171): the record cannot be faulted from a retry wait, so that path has no skip. A first version of the test that expected a cancellation timed out after 15 s with the receive still running (30 s retry delays). The comment in `ConsumePipeline` that said MassTransit stops retrying at shutdown was wrong and is corrected. Cost: a stop can be held by the rest of the schedule, at most `Kafka:Consumers` RetryCount (3) times RetryMaxMilliseconds (5,000), plus the attempts, plus the dead letter.
- Tests written (2026-10-13): unit `DeadLetterOutboxTests` (fit with long non-ASCII headers and with a huge key, an ordinary letter whole, row id and key, the keep path, the failing store, the store that never answers ended at `KeepTimeout`, the relay's topic check) and three `ConsumePipelineTests` (keep and complete with and without retries; store failing; the stop during a retry wait), 67 of 67 messaging unit tests three times; integration `DeadLetterKeptAtStopTests` (poison and unreadable) and `DeadLetterShutdownTests` (now three cases: stop, dispose, and the database cut too). First integration run: all five failed on test faults, not on the change: DeadLetterShutdownTests ran its hosts with the relay off, so the kept row was never sent; its probe text "kept in the outbox" is also inside "could not be kept in the outbox either"; and its database-cut case asserted before restoring Postgres while its `finally` restored only Kafka, so DeadLetterKeptAtStopTests then ran with the database cut (the inbox claims failed, so the later record never reached the consumer). The product logs showed the intended path each time ("not sent before messaging stopped; kept in the outbox, which sends it later" at the stops with the database up). Fixed in the tests.
- Second run (15:33 to 15:39): 4 of 5 passed (DeadLetterShutdownTests all three cases; DeadLetterKeptAtStopTests poison). The unreadable case failed on the test: MassTransit's `KafkaMessageConsumer` pushes each record to a `PartitionChannelExecutorPool` of `ConcurrentMessageLimit` (8) lanes chosen by a Murmur3 hash of the record key (`MassTransit.Middleware.Murmur3UnsafeHashGenerator`), one message at a time per lane, so the slow record's key had landed in the poison record's lane and waited behind it. The test now picks the later and slow keys outside the poison record's lane with MassTransit's own hash. It also sharpens the residual: only a later record of another key in another lane can complete during a dead-letter loop.
- Proven on real Kafka (2026-10-13 15:40 to 15:45, scratchpad 166/171): with the change, DeadLetterKeptAtStopTests passed both cases (the letter kept at the stop, the later record committed past the poison record during the stop, the relay of the next host sending the letter about a second after it started, every record committed, the poison record not delivered again). With the store left out of `ConsumePipeline` (a temporary build, source restored), both cases failed exactly on the skip: the committed offset was already past the poison record (the later record checkpointed during the stop, the first assertion passed) and the poison record had been faulted ("left unacknowledged"), so it would never come back and had no dead letter. DeadLetterShutdownTests passed its three cases (the second run).
- Docs (2026-10-13): ADR-0018 gains a dated ARV-171 note (the ARV-166 note left byte for byte); overview (Producing) describes the keep, the retry-wait behaviour and the residual now needing the database away too; wiki 10 section 4.5a (what operators see, the query for kept letters, the replay check only for the database-away case); CWE-400 row and ASVS V16.5.2 updated with the tests; decisions.md gains an ARV-171 entry with three points pending the owner (no last Kafka attempt at a stop, the 10 second bound, every host registering every dead-letter producer). Gates started 15:47 UTC.
- Gates (2026-10-13 15:47 to 16:29, fresh services, the tree as handed back): `node scripts/verify.mjs backend` exit 0 (PASS dotnet build, golden, unit tests, scanner self-test, security scan, base images, chart security, NuGet and npm audits); `node scripts/verify.mjs story --specs tests/api/device-push.spec.ts --integration "FullyQualifiedName~DeadLetter|...|FullyQualifiedName~QueueStream"` exit 0, widened to the full suites (wide: Ariva.Infra Messaging, Ariva.Di): unit 5,299 passed, integration 517 passed and 1 skipped, E2E 687 passed and 1 skipped; `node scripts/security/scan.mjs --changed` exit 0 (10 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings); `node scripts/verify.mjs docs` exit 0.
- Tallies after the gates (2026-10-13 16:29 to 17:01, one process per run, 16 `yes` hogs, stopped afterwards): DeadLetterKeptAtStopTests 10 of 10 passed (both cases each run, 67 to 74 s a run); DeadLetterShutdownTests 10 of 10 passed (all three cases each run, 116 to 122 s). The security review followed.
- Security review (security-reviewer; CWE-501 message loss and CWE-400, with CWE-89 and CWE-532 judged): PASS (2026-10-13) on code, tests and docs. ARV-166 condition C1 closed: a record whose dead letter Kafka refused at a stop no longer completes without its letter stored durably (the keep is one INSERT committing on its own before the method returns; a bound that fires after the commit faults the record with the letter already durable, and a redelivery adds no second row); housekeeping deletes only sent rows; the relay's topic check keeps a row from being steered to a domain topic; `ariva.dead-letter` cannot collide with an event type; the store's SQL is constant with named parameters; logs name only topic, partition and offset. `scan.mjs --changed` 10 files, 0 errors (the 3 new files scanned explicitly, 0 errors). Follow-ups, none blocking: (1) a NUL or lone surrogate in a record's key, headers or error message makes the keep fail, since PostgreSQL refuses it (sanitise in `DeadLetters.Create`, digest key, test), and meanwhile the residual text names the case (done in ConsumeFilters, overview, the ADR-0018 ARV-171 note and wiki 10 before the commit); (2) a failing `.dlq.v1` row should hold back only its topic, not end the relay pass; (3) `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` 60 and `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` about 50 s on the consuming hosts, since the defaults of 30 s are tight against the retry schedule plus the keep (correctness holds either way); all three in ARV-175; (4) WRITE on every dead-letter topic for each per-service principal, in ARV-083's notes. Passes set to true.

## 2026-10-13 ARV-173 Two interval readings ending at the same instant both land in their own minute (Phase 1, branch story/mvp-phase1)
- Started on 0666feb (tree clean; Stryker of the checkpoint runs in its own worktree). Passes false, pending the security review. Plan in the session scratchpad (173/plan.md); findings are written here as they come.

- Replay heads, old engine against new (2026-10-13 17:58 UTC, a temporary probe; the HEAD engine files put back for one build, then the change restored): identical for all four: AUH-TA 0733ca50055c885282f8f823c94e48d8935c7d9ade7b0f306b4e2edc9fa8d030 (4,383 outputs; no locked file, so checked here), the desk zone case f4887f9603d9d9287dcc5ec85d7c66bd163746237cbf578a3b6da070acef3834 (8,049), golden 2b047dfce6d587d26ac5f99e4dd9c0817627b3b63d21792caf4f0a1cc6abd05e (3,694), overflow 0a38ac8833154f3810780e1360f77996b417fc8c3b04ce422e8bed7dd1ff12a8 (1,966).
